concepts.def: The industrial process that manufactures ammonia from nitrogen and hydrogen. The purified gases are passed over an iron catalyst at about 450 degrees C and about 200 atmospheres.
The compound NH3 made by the Haber process. It is the starting point for nitrogen-based fertilisers, and is not itself spread on fields as the finished fertiliser.
A substance fed into an industrial process. For the Haber process the raw materials are the two reactant gases, nitrogen and hydrogen.
The nitrogen for the Haber process comes from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen.
The hydrogen for the Haber process is obtained from natural gas (methane) or other hydrocarbons.
The catalyst used in the Haber process. It speeds up the rate at which equilibrium is reached but does not change the position of equilibrium, so it does not change the yield.

A reaction in which the products can react to re-form the reactants. In the Haber process some of the ammonia formed breaks down again into nitrogen and hydrogen, so the reaction never goes to completion.

concepts.term: Word equation for the Haber process
concepts.def: The specification states the reaction as: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ ammonia. The double arrow shows that the reaction is reversible.
On cooling, the ammonia condenses to a liquid at a much higher temperature than nitrogen or hydrogen do, so it can be run off and removed while the other two gases stay as gases.
The nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted are passed back into the reactor instead of being wasted, which raises the overall conversion and cuts costs.
How quickly ammonia is produced. Raising the temperature, raising the pressure and adding the iron catalyst all increase the rate.
The state reached in a closed system when the forward and reverse reactions occur at the same rate, so the amounts of nitrogen, hydrogen and ammonia stay constant although both reactions continue.

How far the equilibrium lies towards the products. Raising the pressure moves it towards ammonia because there are fewer gas molecules on the ammonia side; raising the temperature moves it away from ammonia because the forward reaction is exothermic.
The proportion of the nitrogen and hydrogen that is converted into ammonia at equilibrium. A high yield and a high rate need opposite temperatures, which is why a compromise is needed.

The conditions actually used in industry: about 450 degrees C gives a lower yield than a cool reactor would but a workable rate, and about 200 atmospheres gives a lower yield than very high pressure would but avoids the cost and danger of stronger plant.
A fertiliser containing compounds of all three of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, the elements with symbols N, P and K.
A mixture made in fixed proportions so that it does a job. An NPK fertiliser is a formulation of several salts blended to give appropriate percentages of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.
A salt made by reacting ammonia with an acid, for example ammonium nitrate from ammonia and nitric acid, or ammonium sulfate from ammonia and sulfuric acid.
An acid manufactured from ammonia. It is used both to make ammonium nitrate and to treat phosphate rock.
A mined rock containing insoluble phosphate compounds. It supplies phosphorus but cannot be used directly as a fertiliser.
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock are dug out of the ground rather than synthesised. The potassium salts can be used in fertilisers without further reaction.
A fertiliser has to dissolve in water in the soil before a plant root can take it up, which is why insoluble phosphate rock is first converted into soluble salts.
The mixture of calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate made by treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid.
The calcium phosphate made by treating phosphate rock with phosphoric acid.

A laboratory preparation is a batch: one small quantity is made, filtered and crystallised by hand. Industrial fertiliser production runs continuously on a large scale through several integrated processes.

mcqs.q: What is manufactured directly by the Haber process?
options: Ammonia, which is then used to make nitrogen fertilisers
Ammonium nitrate, ready for spreading onto farm fields
Nitric acid, which is sprayed on crops as plant feed
Nitrogen and hydrogen, drawn straight from the air
mcqs.explain: The Haber process manufactures ammonia, and that ammonia is used to produce nitrogen-based fertilisers.

mcqs.q: Which pair of gases are the raw materials for the Haber process?
options: Nitrogen and oxygen gas
Nitrogen and hydrogen
Hydrogen and methane
Hydrogen and oxygen
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the raw materials for the Haber process are nitrogen and hydrogen.

mcqs.q: A student is asked to give a source of the nitrogen used in the Haber process. Which answer is correct?
options: It is obtained from natural gas, together with the hydrogen
It is obtained by heating ammonium salts in large vessels
It is obtained from the air, which is about 78% nitrogen
It is obtained by electrolysis of concentrated brine
mcqs.explain: Air is the source of the nitrogen and is about 78% nitrogen by volume.

mcqs.q: Which is the usual industrial source of the hydrogen used in the Haber process?
options: Electrolysis of water, which splits it into elements
The air, as hydrogen is one of the gases present in it
Heating ammonia so that it splits into its elements
Natural gas, which consists mainly of methane
mcqs.explain: Hydrogen is obtained from natural gas (methane) or from other hydrocarbons.

mcqs.q: Which conditions are used in the Haber process?
options: An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 20 atmospheres
An iron catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
A nickel catalyst, 450 degrees C and 200 atmospheres
An iron catalyst, 45 degrees C and 20 atmospheres
mcqs.explain: The specification gives an iron catalyst, a high temperature of about 450 degrees C and a high pressure of about 200 atmospheres.

mcqs.q: What is the effect of the iron catalyst in the Haber process?
options: It increases the yield of ammonia formed at equilibrium
It is used up slowly and has to be replaced each time
It speeds up the rate at which the equilibrium is reached
It stops the ammonia formed from breaking down again
mcqs.explain: The catalyst raises the rate of the forward and reverse reactions equally, so equilibrium arrives sooner.

mcqs.q: The Haber reaction is reversible. What does this mean inside the reactor?
options: All the nitrogen and hydrogen react, then some ammonia breaks down
The reaction runs forwards during the day and backwards at night
The ammonia formed can never break down once it is made
Some of the ammonia breaks down into nitrogen and hydrogen
mcqs.explain: The specification states that the reaction is reversible, so some of the ammonia produced breaks down again.

mcqs.q: Which equation for the Haber process is written as the specification gives it?
options: nitrogen +hydrogen ⇌ammonia
ammonia ⇌nitrogen + hydrogen
nitrogen + hydrogen → ammonia
nitrogen + hydrogen ⇌ ammonium
mcqs.explain: This is the word equation exactly as the specification states it, with the double arrow for a reversible reaction.

mcqs.q: Which balanced symbol equation represents the Haber process?
options: N2 + 3H2 ⇌ NH3
N + 3H ⇌ NH3
N2 + H2 ⇌ NH3
mcqs.explain: Two nitrogen atoms and six hydrogen atoms appear on each side, so the equation is balanced.

mcqs.q: The mixture leaving the reactor is cooled. What happens?
options: The nitrogen and the hydrogen liquefy and are then drawn off
All three gases liquefy together and are then distilled
The ammonia decomposes back to nitrogen and hydrogen
The ammonia liquefies and is removed from the gas mixture
mcqs.explain: On cooling, the ammonia liquefies and is removed, leaving the other two gases behind.

mcqs.q: What happens to the nitrogen and hydrogen that have not reacted?
options: They are recycled back through the reactor
They are burnt to provide heat for the reactor
They are released into the air as harmless gases
They are cooled and sold as by-products
mcqs.explain: The remaining hydrogen and nitrogen are recycled, so the raw materials are not wasted.

mcqs.q: A graph shows the rate of the Haber reaction against temperature at a fixed pressure. What does it show?
options: The rate falls steadily as the temperature is increased
The rate rises as the temperature is increased
The rate is unchanged by temperature at constant pressure
The rate falls at first and then rises again above 450 C
mcqs.explain: Higher temperature means more frequent and more energetic collisions, so the rate increases.

mcqs.q: A graph shows the percentage yield of ammonia against pressure at 450 degrees C. What is the trend, and why?
options: Yield falls, because squashing the gases hinders the reaction
Yield is constant, because pressure only changes the rate
Yield falls, because ammonia is squeezed back into its elements
Yield rises, because there are fewer gas molecules in the ammonia
mcqs.explain: Four molecules of gas become two, so raising the pressure shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia.

mcqs.q: Inside a sealed Haber reactor at equilibrium, what is true?
options: Both reactions are still going on at the same rate
Both the forward and reverse reactions have stopped
The amounts of all three gases are now equal
Only the forward reaction is taking place
mcqs.explain: At dynamic equilibrium the forward and reverse reactions occur at equal rates, so amounts stay constant.

mcqs.q: Ammonia is removed from the mixture as it liquefies. What is the effect on the equilibrium?
options: There is no effect, since the ammonia has already been made
It shifts towards the ammonia side, so more gas reacts
It shifts back towards the nitrogen and hydrogen instead
It stops the reverse reaction from happening at all
mcqs.explain: Removing a product moves the equilibrium to replace it, raising the overall conversion.

mcqs.q: Why is the Haber process not run at a much lower temperature than 450 degrees C?
options: Because the yield of ammonia would be lower at low temperatures
Because the iron catalyst does not work at all below 450 C
Because the reaction would then be far too slow to use
Because a lower temperature would shift the equilibrium back
mcqs.explain: A low temperature gives a better yield but so slow a rate that the plant would be uneconomic.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the trade-off between rate of production and position of equilibrium?
options: The conditions give the most ammonia per day, not the best yield or the fastest rate
The conditions chosen are simply those that give the fastest possible reaction
The conditions chosen are the ones giving the highest possible yield of ammonia
The catalyst is chosen so that the yield and the rate can both be maximised
mcqs.explain: A compromise temperature accepts a lower equilibrium yield in exchange for a workable rate of production.

mcqs.q: Why is a pressure of about 200 atmospheres used rather than a far higher one?
options: Because a higher pressure would reduce the yield of the ammonia made
Because the iron catalyst is destroyed above 200 atmospheres
Because stronger plant, more energy and greater risk cost more
Because 200 atmospheres gives the greatest possible yield
mcqs.explain: Yield would rise further, but the extra pipework, compression energy and hazard are not worth the gain.

mcqs.q: The nitrogen for the Haber process is taken from the air. Which reason best explains this choice?
options: Nitrogen taken from the air is more reactive than nitrogen from a tank
Air is free and is about 78% nitrogen, so it is the cheapest source
Air already contains all the hydrogen that is needed for the reaction
Nitrogen from the air needs no purification before it is used
mcqs.explain: Commercial conditions and raw materials are chosen for availability and cost, and air costs nothing.

mcqs.q: An NPK fertiliser contains compounds of which three elements?
options: Nitrogen, phosphorus and krypton, symbol K
Nitrogen, potassium and carbon, from K
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium salts
Nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium
mcqs.explain: NPK fertilisers contain compounds of nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium.

mcqs.q: Why is an NPK fertiliser described as a formulation?
options: Because it is one single compound whose formula contains all three elements
Because its salts all dissolve to give exactly the same ions in the soil
Because it is a mixture of salts blended to give set percentages of N, P and K
Because it is made in one reactor from a single mined raw material
mcqs.explain: NPK fertilisers are formulations of various salts containing appropriate percentages of the elements.

mcqs.q: Ammonia from the Haber process can be used to manufacture which substances?
options: Ammonium salts and nitric acid
Ammonium salts and sulfuric acid
Nitric acid and sulfuric acid
Nitric acid and phosphates
mcqs.explain: The specification states that ammonia can be used to manufacture ammonium salts and nitric acid.

mcqs.q: Which of these fertiliser raw materials are obtained by mining?
options: Ammonium nitrate, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock
Potassium chloride and nitric acid, but not phosphate rock
Only phosphate rock, since the potassium salts are made in plants
Potassium chloride, potassium sulfate and phosphate rock
mcqs.explain: The specification lists these three as obtained by mining.

mcqs.q: Why can phosphate rock not be used directly as a fertiliser?
options: Because it is too acidic and would damage the roots of the crop
Because the phosphate compounds in it do not dissolve
Because it contains far too little phosphorus to be of any use
Because it dissolves so readily that the rain washes it away
mcqs.explain: Plant roots take up dissolved ions, so the insoluble phosphate must first be made into soluble salts.

mcqs.q: Phosphate rock is treated with sulfuric acid. What is produced?
options: Calcium sulfate only, with the phosphate left in the rock
Calcium phosphate only, known as triple superphosphate
Ammonium sulfate, which supplies nitrogen and sulfur
Single superphosphate: calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
mcqs.explain: Treating phosphate rock with sulfuric acid gives single superphosphate, a mixture of the two salts.

mcqs.q: Phosphate rock is treated with nitric acid. Which products are formed?
options: Ammonium nitrate and calcium oxide
Phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate
Calcium phosphate and calcium sulfate
Calcium nitrate and calcium oxide
mcqs.explain: Treating phosphate rock with nitric acid produces phosphoric acid and calcium nitrate.

mcqs.q: Which salt is produced when phosphate rock is treated with phosphoric acid?
options: Calcium phosphate, called triple superphosphate
Calcium sulfate, the salt in single superphosphate
Calcium phosphate mixed with some calcium sulfate
Ammonium phosphate, made from the rock alone
mcqs.explain: Phosphoric acid converts phosphate rock into calcium phosphate, known as triple superphosphate.

mcqs.q: A student makes ammonium sulfate in the laboratory by titration and crystallisation. How does industrial production of the same salt differ?
options: It uses different chemicals, because the laboratory acids are too weak
It is carried out in exactly the same way, but with larger apparatus
It runs continuously on a large scale, with reactants recycled
It produces a purer product, because no crystallisation is needed
mcqs.explain: Industrial production is continuous, large scale and integrated, whereas the laboratory prepares a single small batch.

mcqs.q: In a Haber reactor at 200 atmospheres the rate of production is 9, 21 and 33 tonnes per hour at 350, 450 and 550 degrees C. The percentage yield at the same three temperatures is 55, 28 and 12. What do the data show?
options: The yield rises with temperature and the rate falls
The rate rises with temperature while the yield falls
Both the rate and the yield fall at higher temperatures
The rate and the yield are both highest at 450 degrees C
mcqs.explain: The rate figures rise from 9 to 33 while the yield figures fall from 55 to 12.

mcqs.q: At 450 degrees C the rate of ammonia production is 12 tonnes per hour at 100 atmospheres, 24 at 200 atmospheres and 45 at 400 atmospheres. What do these data show?
options: The rate falls as the gases are squashed up
The rate stops rising beyond 200 atmospheres
Raising the pressure does not change the rate
Doubling the pressure roughly doubles the rate
mcqs.explain: 12 to 24 and 24 to 45: each doubling of the pressure roughly doubles the rate of production.
